item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=theoretical+frameworks+for+artificial+moral+agency+and+responsibility+attribution+in+autonomous+systems&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7473639\", \"title\": [\"Artificial Intelligence and Legal Responsibility: Agency, Causal Attribution, Foreseeability and the Reconstruction of Liability in Autonomous Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Contemporary liability doctrine addresses artificial intelligence through three analytically separate inquiries: agency doctrine, which asks who authorized an act; causal-attribution doctrine, which asks what produced a harm; and foreseeability doctrine, which asks what a reasonable actor should have anticipated. Each inquiry anchors its analysis to a different moment in a system's lifecycle-delegation, harm, and design, respectively. For conventional tools this temporal separation is harmless because a single human actor typically occupies all three positions at once. Autonomous systems break that coincidence: the interval between design, delegation, and harm now contains machine-generated intervening choices that no human actor directly authorized, observed, or could fully anticipate. This article develops the thesis that recent liability reforms-the European Union's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the United Kingdom's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the Republic of Korea's Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, and Brazil's pending Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023)-each stabilize only one of these three temporal anchors without reconciling how the anchors interact when a single harm implicates all three simultaneously. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis across these four jurisdictions plus United States tort doctrine, the article identifies this structural problem as temporal anchor divergence: the three liability inquiries increasingly point to different responsible parties for the same harm rather than converging on one, and current reforms treat this divergence as an implementation detail rather than a problem requiring an explicit resolution rule.
